beats.beat: At Mrs Pike's dinner, Miss Marchmont arrives plainly dressed and more curious about the old house's library than about being introduced to anyone.
Rowe, coached beforehand, is stiff and overpraises everything within reach, and Louisa remains polite but plainly unmoved.
Louisa and Judith fall into easy talk about a book both have read, and Mrs Pike, watching them laugh, decides this proves Louisa charmed by the evening, and therefore by Rowe.
beats.note: Mrs Pike's line implies success of the evening generally; her crediting it specifically to Rowe is inferred rather than stated.

beats.beat: Alone with Judith afterward, Louisa admits she has come to persuade her uncle to give the empty house a use, not to be courted by anyone, and asks what the parish truly needs.
Judith answers plainly: a schoolroom, since the old one is falling in, and watches an idea take hold in Louisa's face.
beats.note: Shown through Louisa's stillness and closing question rather than named directly, which is the stronger choice.

turn.note: Louisa's 'How many children?' signals her intent to act on the schoolroom idea, redirecting the story from courtship comedy to the estate rescuing the roof.

problems: The triple 'He said that... and then that... and then... that' construction is a rule-of-three list padded to three parallel clauses; trim to two or let the third change shape more sharply to earn its length.

borrowed_text: "The Orphan of Kerrow" sits uncomfortably close to "The Orphan of the Rhine," a real Gothic novel named in Austen's own horrid-novels list; the resemblance risks reading as lifted rather than invented.
trope_note: The meddling matchmaker is delivered straight and well here, with Mrs Pike misreading a literary joke as romantic success; enemies of manner sits dormant this chapter since Rowe and Judith do not speak directly, which is acceptable given the outline distributes the beats across chapters.
fixes: Rewrite the opening sentence: 'the guest arrived in the same brown she had travelled down in' assumes a detail (her arrival, her dress) never shown on the page. Name her directly and drop the false callback: e.g. 'Mrs Pike had settled everything but the guest, and Miss Louisa Marchmont arrived in a plain brown gown, her boots wet from cutting across the glebe rather than coming by the road.'
Rename or alter 'The Orphan of Kerrow' to something further from 'The Orphan of the Rhine' so it reads as invented parody rather than borrowed title.
Trim the three-part 'prospect... prospect... weather' sentence to two items, or sharpen the third so the joke lands as escalation rather than a rule-of-three list.
Make Mrs Pike's misreading explicit to fully land the matchmaker beat: have her line name Rowe outright, e.g. 'There. You see how well they take to each other, and I said Mr Rowe would do it.'

findings.quote: He said that the prospect from the gatehouse windows was uncommonly fine, and then that the prospect from the green was uncommonly fine, and...
findings.note: 41 words in one sentence. A listener cannot re-read it. Split it, or cut it to under 40.

writer_note:
This story is now read by a single narrator rather than a
cast with a voice each, so the prose has to carry who is speaking. It was
written under the old rule, which forbade attribution because the voices made it
redundant.

Go through the chapter and add attribution wherever a listener — who cannot see
the page, and cannot look back — would lose track of who is speaking. A tag
belongs in its own narrator segment: `said Mrs Pike`, `Rowe said`, or an action
that does the same work: *Rowe turned the note over.* Two people alternating in
a plain exchange do not need one every line; the third turn usually does, and so
does every return to dialogue after narration, and every line in a scene of
three or more.

Do not attribute every line. An unbroken column of `said X` is padding, and it
is the opposite failure.

Where a line would be misread without it, you may add a `tag` to that segment —
`"[quietly]"`, `"[a beat]"`, `"[warmly]"` — as performance direction for the
voice. It is never printed and never spoken. A few a chapter at most, and never
to imitate a different person: one voice reads everyone.

Come back no longer than you started. These chapters are already at or over
their word ceiling, and attribution adds words — so take them back out of
restatement: a line of dialogue that lands followed by narration explaining that
it landed, a room established twice. If you come back long the check sends the
chapter straight back to be cut, which spends a revision on arithmetic instead
of on the prose.

Change nothing else. Same events, same beats, same jokes, same last line.
